source: Lewis and Durrant (2011) Overlapping memory replay during sleep builds cognitive schemata
finding: Founding proposal (iOtA, information overlap to abstract). Related memories are replayed in overlapping combinations in slow wave sleep. Replay strengthens the elements they share, so shared structure (gist) grows and unique detail does not. Repeated replay in new combinations builds schemas. The same mechanism is said to explain insight and false memory.
numbers: Abstract only read this session. No new data; a theory paper. Mechanism: Hebbian strengthening of overlap plus later general forgetting of detail.
quote: Overlapping replay of related memories selectively strengthens shared elements.
limits: Theory is not tested directly in humans at synapse level. Evidence is indirect (behaviour plus sleep staging). No direct recording of overlapping-set replay in humans.
agent_relevance: Subgoal library: when several solved cases share a rule fragment, strengthen the shared fragment and let the case-specific parts decay. Merge by overlap, not by storing every case.

source: Lewis, Knoblich and Poe (2018) How memory replay in sleep boosts creative problem-solving
finding: Restates iOtA and extends it to BiOtA. Non-REM: hippocampus biases the cortex to replay thematically linked memories together, so overlap is potentiated and gist forms. REM: hippocampus and cortex decouple, random PGO input activates unrelated cortical schemas together, so structure shared between whole schemas (atom and solar system) can be found. Order matters: non-REM first to form schemas, REM second to link them. Repeated cycles push content into deeper, more compressed layers.
numbers: Proposed network: hippocampal nodes, a first cortical layer trained by non-REM replay (Rumelhart-style backprop, groups similar items), a third layer trained by REM replay of layer one. Non-REM replay is 6-20x faster than real time. DRM results on sleep: facilitate (refs 28-31), suppress (ref 32), no change (ref 33).
quote: If these schemas are replayed concurrently in REM sleep, the shared structure will be detected
limits: Computational model is hypothetical, not run. REM role is the least supported part. DRM gist results are mixed and may test a different mechanism because the gist word was never learned.
agent_relevance: Two-stage consolidation for the rule library: stage 1 merges cases inside one family into a rule; stage 2 compares whole rules across families to find cross-domain structure. Do stage 1 before stage 2. An autoencoder-style check (can the compressed rule rebuild the cases) tells which cases need more replay.

source: Lewis, Knoblich and Poe (2018), box on replay physiology
finding: Replay facts the theory leans on. Rat place-cell replay: a 20 s track run is replayed in about 200 ms in non-REM. Replay occurs tens to hundreds of times a night, more for salient or recent items. Disrupting sharp wave ripples causes a rebound in ripples. Evidence for gist in sleep cited: statistical learning, object property generalisation, grammar learning, infant word generalisation, number reduction task, cued replay of an implicit sequence giving explicit knowledge.
numbers: 20 s to 200 ms is about 100x compression in the example shown; general range 6-20x. Ripples 150-300 Hz, slow waves about 0.8 Hz.
limits: Rodent place-cell replay is not replay of overlapping memory sets; the step from rat trajectory replay to human gist is an inference.
agent_relevance: Replay is salience weighted. Weight which solved cases get re-examined by outcome value or surprise, not uniformly.

source: Wagner, Gais, Haider, Verleger and Born (2004) Sleep inspires insight
finding: Number reduction task with a hidden abstract rule. After 8 h of nocturnal sleep, more than twice as many subjects gained insight into the hidden rule than after nocturnal or daytime wakefulness. No effect without initial training. Reaction times slowed across sleep before insight.
numbers: Abstract: more than twice as many subjects gained insight after sleep. Review table lists N = 106 adults, overnight, explicit effect yes. Exact percentages not read this session.
limits: Abstract only. Later work (Debarnot 2017, N=74) found the effect in young but not in old adults. Task has a rule shared across all trials, so overlap is maximal.
agent_relevance: Hidden shared rules in a case set are found more often after an offline consolidation pass than by continuing the same search. Suggests a separate consolidation step after a batch of cases, not only inline rule guessing.

source: Durrant, Taylor, Cairney and Lewis (2011) Sleep-dependent consolidation of statistical learning
finding: Tone sequences with a hidden probabilistic structure. Test is recognition of novel short sequences that fit the same pattern. Overnight sleep beat daytime wake. A 4 h nap beat 4 h of wake. Improvement correlated with slow wave sleep amount. Also a time-based consolidation component independent of sleep.
numbers: Review table: N = 36 adults, overnight, implicit effect yes, SWS correlate. Exact r not read this session.
limits: Abstract only. Later replications by the same group (nap, 2012/2016, N=48) and cueing (Hennies 2017, N=42). Not an independent lab. Time-based effect shows sleep is not the only route.
agent_relevance: Gist of a statistical pattern improves with offline time. A rule library should be rebuilt from stored cases after a delay, not only at the moment of solving.

source: Durrant, Cairney, McDermott and Lewis (2013) Overnight consolidation aids the transfer of statistical knowledge from the medial temporal lobe to the striatum
finding: Same tone paradigm with fMRI. Greater improvement across 24 h than across 30 min, predicted by SWS. After sleep, parahippocampal response weaker and striatal response stronger. Striatum-parahippocampus connectivity weaker after sleep.
numbers: Exact N and statistics not read this session.
limits: Abstract only. Neural account: abstracted knowledge moves from hippocampal to striatal system.
agent_relevance: Abstracted rules should be stored where they can be applied without recalling the original cases. Keep the rule, allow the cases to be dropped.

source: Ellenbogen, Hu, Payne, Titone and Walker (2007) Human relational memory requires time and sleep (as reported in Lerner and Gluck 2019 review)
finding: Transitive inference with six items A>B>C>D>E>F. Only adjacent pairs trained. Inference pairs (BD, CE, BE) were better after sleep than wake, but explicit knowledge of the hierarchy was not improved. Replicated by Werchen and Gomez 2013 (N=64, overnight, implicit effect yes, explicit no).
numbers: Review table entry: N = 56 adults, overnight, implicit yes, explicit no. Original paper not opened; percent-correct figures not verified.
limits: Seen only through a review. The sleep gain shows in implicit performance, not explicit rule report.
agent_relevance: Inference between never-paired items is a test of whether merged structure exists. Use held-out inference pairs (G3) as the check on a merged subgoal.

source: Lau et al. (2010) nap and associative inference; Alger and Payne (2016) (as reported in Lerner and Gluck 2019)
finding: Lau: a nap improved direct (A-B, B-C) and indirect (A-C) associations; the indirect gain correlated with SWS amount (N=31). Alger and Payne replicated the nap effect with neutral and emotional images (N=58) but the correlate was REM, not SWS.
numbers: N=31 and N=58 from the review table.
limits: The sleep stage that carries the effect flips between a study and its replication (SWS vs REM). So stage-specific claims are weak.
agent_relevance: Do not hard-code a single merge mechanism. Treat stage-specific roles as unsettled.

source: Lerner and Gluck (2019) Sleep and the extraction of hidden regularities: a systematic review
finding: Many null results exist. Which task was used predicted a sleep effect better than the cognitive process or the design. Explicit detection of hidden rules was more likely when the rule was temporal (A at t predicts B later) than non-temporal. Tied to compressed replay in SWS.
numbers: Table covers dozens of studies. Examples: Wagner N=106; Ellenbogen N=56; Durrant 2011 N=36; SRTT studies with N 16-161. Many SRTT and ASRT rows show No for explicit effect (Song 2007 N=36, Hallgato 2013 N=102).
quote: the explicit detection of hidden rules is more likely to happen when the rules are of a temporal nature
limits: Systematic review, not a meta-analysis; no pooled effect size. Non-temporal, prior-knowledge based abstraction seems to rely on REM or cortex rather than SWS.
agent_relevance: Gist from sequences (order-dependent rules) is the best supported case. For our agent, the strongest case for merging is across ordered solution traces, with weaker support for merging unordered facts.

source: Lerner and Gluck (2019), category and prototype studies in the review
finding: For category learning and prototype generalisation after sleep results are mixed: one study found sleep helped categorisation, one found no immediate gain but a larger gain after retraining, one found nothing. An explicit generation test showed no sleep effect. No study linked generalisation directly to SWS. Two studies linked REM to memory for trained exemplars, not to generalisation. Three infant studies using one paradigm linked it to spindles and N2.
numbers: Counts as stated in the review text; no pooled statistics.
limits: Heterogeneous tasks; small samples; some tests were contaminated by earlier exposure to prototypes.
agent_relevance: Expect gist merging to help some tasks and be neutral on others. Measure it per task type at equal tokens (G7).

source: Lutz, Diekelmann, Hinse-Stern, Born and Rauss (2017) Sleep supports the slow abstraction of gist from visual perceptual memories
finding: Visual DRM with shape sets built from an unseen prototype. At 10 h, sleep raised memory for single old items (high-confidence old shapes, t(12)=2.27, p=0.043, eta2=0.30) but not prototype (gist) memory (t(12)=-0.08). One year later (N=17), only prototypes encoded before sleep were above chance (t(16)=6.25, p<0.001, eta2=0.71); old items were at chance.
numbers: Encoded 16 sets of 10 shapes per condition (160 shapes each). Short group N=15 (20 min), long group N=13 (10 h). REM time correlated with item memory (r=0.61, p=0.027). Planned contrast sleep-prototype vs other three: t(16)=5.75, eta2=0.67.
quote: effective gist abstraction is thought to require multiple nights
limits: Small N; 17 of 28 returned at one year. Gist effect appears only after a long delay, not overnight. Contradicts the idea that one night is enough for gist. Correlations between sleep stage and one-year gist were null (|r|<0.34).
agent_relevance: Gist advantage can be invisible right after consolidation and show only later. Evaluate a merged-rule library after many tasks, not at the next task.

source: Sweegers and Talamini (2014) Generalization from episodic memories across time
finding: Face-location associations with a hidden regularity. Generalisation to new items improved across a 4 h post-learning period. No difference between sleep and wake in that period. Regularity extraction hurt memory for arbitrary facial features. Over several weeks regularity memory stayed robust while arbitrary associations were forgotten steeply.
numbers: Abstract only; N not read.
limits: Failed sleep-specific effect: time passed helped regardless of sleep state. The tradeoff (gist gain, detail loss) matches iOtA.
agent_relevance: Merging costs detail: after extracting a rule, specifics of single cases are poorer. Keep a small raw-case archive if details may be needed.

source: Hennies, Ralph, Kempkes, Cairney and Lewis (2016) Sleep spindle density predicts the effect of prior knowledge on memory consolidation
finding: Schema (arthropods or cell biology) built over 2 weeks. New facts related to the schema decayed less overnight in people with higher N2 spindle density. Regression with spindle density and SWS predicted 56.2% of variance in the overnight schema effect (F(5,13)=5.63, p=0.006). Hippocampal disengagement across 24 h appeared only for schema-related memories.
numbers: Schema group N=23 (19 in regression), control group N=24 (strong vs weak encoding). Spindle density t=4.11, p=0.001; SWS t=-3.05, p=0.009. Median split three-way interaction F(17)=22.12, p<0.001. For unrelated facts no difference, F(17)=0.69.
limits: Correlational (no sleep deprivation arm). SWS and N2 were collinear so they cannot be separated. Small N. The mechanism here is integration of new items into an existing schema, not extraction of a new one.
agent_relevance: New cases that fit an existing rule consolidate better. Place a new case against existing rules first; if it fits, attach it; if not, keep it separate until it can be tested.

source: Tse et al. (2007) Schemas and memory consolidation
finding: Rats learned flavour-place paired associates. After a schema had gradually formed, a new association learned in one trial became hippocampus-independent very quickly. The schema was also needed for lasting memory of one-trial learning.
numbers: Numbers not read this session (abstract only).
limits: Rodent, abstract only. Shows consolidation speed depends on schema presence.
agent_relevance: A rule library speeds later learning: cases that match an existing rule need less rehearsal. Supports building the library before it is needed.

source: McClelland, McNaughton and OReilly (1995) Why there are complementary learning systems
finding: Connectionist account. Cortical networks find structure only if learning is slow and interleaved across many items. Fast learning of a new item alone causes catastrophic interference. The hippocampus learns fast and reinstates memories to the cortex, interleaving new with old.
numbers: Abstract only. Simulation numbers not read.
limits: Predicts that gist extraction needs interleaved replay, not massed new learning. Nothing about sleep staging.
agent_relevance: Do not rewrite the rule library from one new case. Interleave the new case with old ones when updating, or the library drifts.

source: Kumaran, Hassabis and McClelland (2016) What learning systems do intelligent agents need? CLS updated
finding: Updated CLS. Replay allows goal-dependent weighting of experience statistics. Hippocampal recurrence can support some generalisation. Neocortical learning can be fast for information consistent with known structure. Explicit link to design of AI agents.
numbers: Abstract only.
limits: Weakens the strict claim that only slow cortical replay generalises.
agent_relevance: Weight replay by goal relevance. Cases consistent with a known rule can be merged fast; novel ones need slow, interleaved handling.

source: Schapiro, Turk-Browne, Botvinick and Norman (2017) Complementary learning systems within the hippocampus
finding: Neural network model of hippocampal subfields. The monosynaptic pathway (EC to CA1) did statistical learning (regularities); the trisynaptic pathway (EC-DG-CA3-CA1) learned single episodes. Apparent regularities in the trisynaptic route came from recurrence and associative reactivation. Covers pair structure, community structure and associative or transitive inference.
numbers: Model uses error-driven plus Hebbian learning (Contrastive Hebbian Learning). No sleep manipulation; this is rapid wake learning over minutes to hours.
limits: Model only; not a sleep account. Predicts a hippocampal route to rapid regularity learning that does not need sleep.
agent_relevance: Two stores in the agent: a verbatim case log and a separate rule summary. Keep them separate so that summarising does not damage case recall.

source: Liu, Dolan, Kurth-Nelson and Behrens (2019) Human replay spontaneously reorganizes experience
finding: MEG in two studies. After learning a rule that orders objects, new objects shown in scrambled order were replayed in rest in the rule-implied order, not the seen order (peak at 40 ms lag, sequenceness beta=0.017+-0.005, N=21). Reverse replay appeared after reward (17/21 reverse). Replay held a factorised code (sequence identity and position) 50 ms before the object code.
numbers: Study 1 N=21, forward replay in 16/21; Study 2 N=22, 17/22 forward. Lags 20-60 ms exceeded corrected threshold p<0.042. Lasso logistic decoders peaked at 200 ms (37.16% +-3.0%).
quote: replay did not simply recapitulate visual experience, but followed instead a sequence implied by learned abstract knowledge
limits: Awake rest, not sleep. MEG sequence detection is statistical and debated. Shows replay applies learned structure to new items, which is the abstraction step but not overlap-driven strengthening.
agent_relevance: Strong human evidence that replay is structure-guided. Matches a design where a stored abstract rule re-orders or relabels new cases before they are filed (factorise structure from content).

source: van de Ven, Siegelmann and Tolias (2020) Brain-inspired replay for continual learning
finding: Generative replay (replay generated by the network itself) works on toy tasks but fails on natural images. Replaying hidden-layer representations from context-modulated feedback connections fixes it. On split CIFAR-100 in the class-incremental setting, existing no-storage methods (GR, EWC, SI, LwF) suffered severe forgetting; brain-inspired replay plus SI reached reasonable accuracy.
numbers: Split CIFAR-100: 10 tasks of 10 classes, 10 repetitions, mean +-SEM. Permuted MNIST (100 tasks): SI ~82%, online EWC ~70%, XdG ~61% (Masse et al.); plain GR did not scale.
limits: Exact BI-R accuracy not read from figure. Replay in this work protects old tasks; it does not extract shared structure.
agent_relevance: Replay of compressed internal representations beats replay of raw inputs. For an LLM agent, replay stored rule summaries, not whole transcripts.

source: Tadros, Krishnan, Ramyaa and Bazhenov (2022) Sleep-like unsupervised replay reduces catastrophic forgetting in artificial neural networks
finding: Sleep phase after each task: offline unsupervised Hebbian plasticity with noisy input (sleep replay consolidation, SRC). Recovers forgotten old tasks. Toy test: four 10x10 binary images, task overlap 12-16 pixels, where the old task was forgotten after task 2 and SRC recovered it. Spontaneous replay formed class-specific representations.
numbers: CUB-200 two tasks: baseline 5% first / 95% second; with SRC 63.2% / 45.4%. CIFAR-10: SRC 44% overall vs 19% control. 5 trials, different inits and task orders.
limits: Overlapping inputs are the source of interference here, and sleep repairs it: overlap is a problem, not a feature. Accuracy still far below parallel training.
agent_relevance: Overlap between old and new rules can cause overwrite. A consolidation pass that revisits old rules after new ones can restore them.

source: Ellis et al. (2020) DreamCoder: growing generalizable, interpretable knowledge with wake-sleep Bayesian program learning
finding: Not an LLM, but the closest computational use of the idea. Wake: solve tasks. Sleep-abstraction: replay solved programs, find common fragments, refactor them into new library primitives that shorten description length. Sleep-dreaming: train a recognition network on replayed and imagined tasks. Library grows in layers.
numbers: Text editing: trained on 128 tasks, tested on 108 SyGuS tasks; solved 3.7% before learning, 79.6% after, in 40 s average vs 235 s; CVC4 82.4% (1 h, 8 CPUs), DreamCoder 84.3% with that budget. LOGO graphics and tower building: nearly 100% held-out vs no baseline above 60%. Physics: after 8 wake-sleep cycles learned 93% of laws and identities. Training about a day on 20-100 CPUs.
quote: replaying experiences from waking, finding common program fragments from task solutions, and abstracting out these fragments into new code primitives
limits: Needs a well-defined program language and a compression score. Gains come from both abstraction and dreaming parts (ablations).
agent_relevance: Direct template for the subgoal library: replay solved cases, extract the shared fragment, add it as a named subgoal if it lowers total description length, then use it in later search. Cost is real compute.

source: Grand et al. (2024) LILO: learning interpretable libraries by compressing and documenting code
finding: LLM writes programs; Stitch compresses solved programs into library functions; an LLM documents each function (AutoDoc). Beats DreamCoder on REGEX (+33.14), LOGO (+20.42), CLEVR (+2.26 on a base of 94.50). Beats the LLM-only solver by +0.94 (REGEX), +8.09 (CLEVR), +16.82 (LOGO). Without library learning the LLM solver beat DreamCoder by +32.20 on REGEX.
numbers: Domains: REGEX, CLEVR, LOGO. Learns the concept of a vowel, which otherwise needs search over 265 disjunctions. An LLM asked to do the compression itself produced valid expressions in only 19.01% (998/5250) of generations (REGEX 24.93%, CLEVR 24.20%, LOGO 4.93%) and compression stayed near 1.0x.
limits: LLM compression was poor; the symbolic compressor (Stitch) did the real merging. Run means over several seeds; not all table cells read.
agent_relevance: Use code (not the model) to find overlapping fragments across solved cases (G5), then let the model name and document the fragment. A model asked to merge rules unaided made mostly invalid abstractions.

source: Lin, Snell, Wang, Packer, Wooders, Stoica and Gonzalez (2025) Sleep-time compute
finding: Let the model think offline about a context before any query arrives. Cuts test-time compute needed for the same accuracy about 5x on Stateful GSM-Symbolic and Stateful AIME. Scaling sleep-time compute raises accuracy up to 13% (GSM) and 18% (AIME). Sharing it across several related queries on one context cut average cost per query 2.5x. Works better when the query is predictable.
numbers: Multi-Query GSM-Symbolic: 2.5x lower cost per query. Case study on an agentic SWE task.
limits: Offline thinking is about precomputing inferences about a context; it does not specifically merge overlapping cases. Gain depends on query predictability.
agent_relevance: Offline consolidation between tasks can be paid once and reused over related tasks. Supports a between-task consolidation pass whose cost is amortised.

source: Lerner and Gluck (2019), null results and replication status
finding: The sleep-and-abstraction literature is not uniform. SRTT rows in the review table show an explicit rule gain in some (Wilhelm 2013 N=161, Lutz 2018 N=117) and none in others (Song 2014 N=40, Hallgato 2013 N=102). Number reduction task: yes in Wagner and Yordanova, no in older adults (Debarnot 2017).
numbers: Counts from the review table.
limits: Task, age and rule type all moderate results. No meta-analytic effect size is given.
agent_relevance: Treat the claim that overlap replay builds gist as plausible but task dependent. Use as design inspiration, not as proof.

source: Winocur and Moscovitch (2011) Memory transformation and systems consolidation
finding: Transformation hypothesis: episodic hippocampal memories become semantic or gist-like in cortex. If episodic detail is retained it still needs the hippocampus; gist does not.
numbers: Abstract only.
limits: Competes with standard consolidation theory in which memories move unchanged.
agent_relevance: Two memory forms: keep case-level episodes and rule-level gist as separate items with separate retrieval paths.

source: Lewis, Knoblich and Poe (2018), proposed testable predictions
finding: Non-REM should come first for efficiency; hippocampal-cortical decoupling in REM leaves hippocampus and cortex ending in different states, to be reconciled in the next non-REM episode (like two researchers working apart then rejoining). Schemas for salient problems are more likely to reactivate. Compression: storage is more compact if similar concepts are coded together.
numbers: No new data. Mentions schizophrenia link with abnormal spindles.
limits: Speculative. No direct test of interleaved order exists in the paper.
agent_relevance: Alternate two passes: merge within family, then cross-compare across families, then reconcile. Order is a testable ablation.
